first_impression.reaction: Googled 'wedding flowers in season' because my fiancee wants peonies and I want to know if that's going to blow the budget. The intro is plain and doesn't oversell, so I kept going. Jumped to the FAQ, then the imported section. The Bureau of Meteorology and Department of Agriculture links, with an 'as at' date, are the kind of sourcing I want. The catch: the title says 'by month' and I expected a list of what's in season each month. What I got is a list of questions to ask the florist. Useful, but not what the headline promised. And there's not one dollar figure anywhere, not even a rough idea of what going imported adds.

journey.quote: Choosing wedding flowers in season starts with a date, not a mood board.
journey.reaction: Good opener. Practical, not gushing. Fine, keep reading.

journey.section: Why choose wedding flowers in season
journey.quote: Petals hold their shape, stems drink well, and arrangements last through a long evening rather than tiring by the speeches.
journey.reaction: Sounds nice, but where's this from? Every other claim on the page has a source and this one is just written like a florist's brochure.

journey.section: Why choose wedding flowers in season
journey.quote: Stems that grow at the same time of year tend to share a mood: the colour of the light, the warmth or coolness of the day, the feel of the venue.
journey.reaction: Mood, light, feel. This is the emotional filler I skip. Tells me nothing I can act on.

journey.section: How the seasons run in Australia
journey.quote: For Australia, the Bureau starts each season on the first of the month: 1 March, 1 June, 1 September and 1 December.
journey.reaction: Sourced, specific, and the wet/dry tropics note is something I wouldn't have thought of. Checks out against BoM.

journey.section: Wedding flowers in season in Australia by month
journey.quote: What grows well in a given month varies with the region, the grower and the year, so the month notes below are about the conversation rather than a fixed list.
journey.reaction: So there's no list. The headline says 'by month' and this is where I find out I'm getting questions instead of flowers. I respect not guessing, but it should say so plainly, up front, not tucked into a soft sentence.

journey.section: Wedding flowers in season in Australia by month
journey.quote: Mid February brings Valentine's Day, one of the peak demand periods in the flower trade.
journey.reaction: Actually useful. Demand drives price, so that's a week to avoid or at least ask about. More of this, please.

journey.section: Wedding flowers in season in Australia by month
journey.quote: For ideas across the cooler months, see our winter flower ideas.
journey.reaction: Hovered the link and the address has '2015' in it. If I click through to a ten-year-old post, that's a credibility hit for the whole site.

journey.section: Wedding flowers in season in Australia by month
journey.quote: If you would like help shaping the whole day around your month, start with Wedded Concierge.
journey.reaction: Sales pitch halfway through, before you've told me anything about what it costs or how you're paid. Easy to ignore, but noted.

journey.quote: As at November 2026, the Department of Agriculture's import conditions require importers to manage biosecurity risk before they send cut flowers and foliage to Australia.
journey.reaction: Dated, government source, and it doesn't pretend the couple needs to deal with it. This is the best section on the page.

journey.quote: Agree in writing which flowers are essential to you and which the florist may substitute.
journey.reaction: This is exactly what I needed last time with a vendor and didn't have. Concrete, protects me. Trust up.

journey.quote: A good local florist will translate that mood into the flowers of their own season.
journey.reaction: Who finds me the 'good' one, and how do I know they're good? That's the whole question with an overseas supplier, and the page skips it.

journey.section: Planning your flowers and spend with your florist
journey.quote: An imported stem, a flower at the edge of its season or a date in a peak week can change a quote, and so can scale, labour and set-up.
journey.reaction: Honest that these things move the price, but 'can change a quote' by how much? No numbers, and the answer is pushed to another article. At minimum tell me how to get the quote broken down so I can see it.

journey.section: Planning your flowers and spend with your florist
journey.quote: With Wedded Concierge, you have one Wedded Advisor, start to finish, as a single point of contact, and your advisor confirms inclusions in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Inclusions in writing is the right promise. Still nothing on what the advisor costs or whether the florist pays you a referral.

journey.quote: Every season has its own character, and none is a poor choice for flowers.
journey.reaction: Dodge. I asked which season suits flowers and got a non-answer. The follow-up line is fine but the first sentence is fluff.
Straight yes-with-a-but answer, then the source. That's how an FAQ should read.

journey.section: Plan your flowers with a Wedded Advisor
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor plans venue, travel, vendors and payments, anywhere in the world, so the flowers sit within a plan that already fits your date and your destination.
journey.reaction: 'Payments' through you means my money goes through your hands to the florist. Do you take a cut? Not answered here.

unanswered_questions: Roughly how much more does an imported stem, or a Valentine's or Christmas week date, add to a flower quote? Even a source-backed range or an example would do.
Which flowers are actually in season each month, beyond waratah in spring? If the brand won't name them, the page should say clearly that it doesn't list stems.
How do I judge whether a florist at an overseas destination is any good? (deferred: supplier vetting)
How is the Wedded Wonderland fee calculated, and what does it buy on the flowers side? (deferred business detail)
Do you take a commission or referral fee from florists, or mark up their prices when payments go through you? (deferred business detail)
Do you source the florist, or do we find our own? (deferred: supplier sourcing)

turn_offs_found.quote: Petals hold their shape, stems drink well, and arrangements last through a long evening rather than tiring by the speeches.
turn_offs_found.why: Confident claim with no source on a page where everything else is sourced. Reads like copy, not fact.

turn_offs_found.quote: Stems that grow at the same time of year tend to share a mood: the colour of the light, the warmth or coolness of the day, the feel of the venue.
What grows well in a given month varies with the region, the grower and the year, so the month notes below are about the conversation rather than a fixed list.
turn_offs_found.why: Headline promises 'by month'; the page softens the fact that it gives no month list. Feels like the catch hidden in nice wording.

turn_offs_found.quote: If you would like help shaping the whole day around your month, start with Wedded Concierge.
turn_offs_found.why: CTA mid-article before any fee or cost information.

turn_offs_found.quote: Every season has its own character, and none is a poor choice for flowers.

would_share_with: My fiancee: the three questions (what is local, what is imported, what is the backup) and the 'agree in writing which flowers are essential' line, before we meet any florist

cta_reaction.quote: Start a conversation through Wedded Concierge.
cta_reaction.why: The page is honest and sourced where it counts, and the 'in writing' advice is exactly my style. But it's a flowers guide with no costs, no month list, and nothing on how you're paid or whether florists pay you. I'd want those answered before I give you my details.

top_3_changes: Say plainly that there is no stem list (stays within 'name no flowers we can't source'). OLD: "What grows well in a given month varies with the region, the grower and the year, so the month notes below are about the conversation rather than a fixed list." NEW: "What grows well in a given month varies with the region, the grower and the year, so this guide does not give a fixed list of stems for each month. Instead, each month below has the questions to ask your florist."

Give me a way to see the cost without inventing numbers. OLD: "An imported stem, a flower at the edge of its season or a date in a peak week can change a quote, and so can scale, labour and set-up." NEW: "An imported stem, a flower at the edge of its season or a date in a peak week can change a quote, and so can scale, labour and set-up. Ask for a quote that shows imported stems, any peak-week surcharge and labour as separate lines, so you can see what each choice costs."

Swap the unsourced brochure line for something actionable. OLD: "Petals hold their shape, stems drink well, and arrangements last through a long evening rather than tiring by the speeches." NEW: "Ask your florist how long each stem will spend between being cut and reaching your venue." Also: replace the FAQ opener "Every season has its own character, and none is a poor choice for flowers." with "No season is wrong for flowers." (fee, commission and florist vetting stay deferred; voiced as unanswered questions only)

open_questions.question: The winter link slug contains '2015' (/7-blooms-you-need-in-your-2015-winter-wedding). Is that post refreshed, or should the link be swapped or its slug redirected? A sceptic who hovers will read it as stale.
Does the source pack hold any sourced figure on peak-week or imported-stem price effects? If so, one number would close the cost objection; if not, the itemised-quote edit is the fallback.

assumptions: Daniel arrived via a Google search for 'wedding flowers in season' while comparing planners; relevance 3 because flowers are a side issue for him, enquiry 2 because no costs and no fee or commission model.
Business details (fees, commissions, florist sourcing and vetting) are deliberately deferred per orchestrator; voiced as unanswered questions only, no edits proposed for them.
Rendered link text and bold labels quoted without markdown syntax, as a reader would see them; the 2015 slug point assumes a hover over the link.
Fast-mode read: intro, FAQ, imported and cost sections read closely; month notes skimmed.
